clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive inborn error of amino acid metabolism caused most often by deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase.
Untreated, accumulation of phenylalanine causes progressive and irreversible intellectual disability, seizures, and behavioural problems.
Affected infants are typically normal at birth, so detection relies on newborn screening rather than clinical signs.
Classic untreated features can include a musty or mousy body odour, eczema, and reduced pigmentation with fair hair and skin.
Early diagnosis through screening and prompt dietary treatment prevent the neurological damage almost entirely.
Treatment centres on a lifelong low-phenylalanine diet with a special protein substitute, guided by regular monitoring of blood phenylalanine levels.
A subset of patients respond to the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (sapropterin), and disorders of biopterin metabolism must be excluded as a separate cause of high phenylalanine.

Maternal PKU with poorly controlled phenylalanine during pregnancy can damage the fetus, causing microcephaly, congenital heart disease, and developmental delay, so strict control is essential before and during pregnancy.
Lifelong follow-up in a metabolic service supports adherence and long-term neurocognitive outcomes.
reference.pathophysiology: Deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (or, less commonly, of its tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor) blocks the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine. Phenylalanine therefore accumulates in blood and tissues and is diverted to alternative metabolites such as phenylketones. High phenylalanine levels are neurotoxic to the developing brain, interfering with amino acid transport across the blood-brain barrier, neurotransmitter synthesis, and myelination, producing the intellectual disability and neurological features of untreated disease. Reduced tyrosine availability also limits synthesis of melanin, contributing to hypopigmentation.
additionalDifferentials: Other inborn errors of metabolism presenting with developmental delay
Non-metabolic causes of intellectual disability and seizures
additionalInvestigations: Newborn bloodspot screening for elevated phenylalanine
Quantitative plasma amino acids (phenylalanine and tyrosine)
Tetrahydrobiopterin loading test and pterin studies to exclude cofactor defects
Genetic analysis of the PAH gene
Serial blood phenylalanine monitoring to guide dietary treatment
redFlags: Markedly elevated phenylalanine levels requiring urgent dietary intervention
Seizures or neurological deterioration in an untreated infant
Poor metabolic control during pregnancy (maternal PKU) risking fetal harm
Failure of phenylalanine to fall despite dietary treatment, suggesting a cofactor defect
Signs of nutritional deficiency from an overly restricted diet
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and consistent dietary control, cognitive development is normal or near-normal; delayed treatment or poor lifelong control leads to irreversible neurocognitive impairment, and maternal control critically affects offspring.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal newborn appearance excludes the diagnosis
Failing to exclude tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency as a treatable alternative cause
Relaxing dietary control in older children and adults, risking cognitive and neuropsychiatric effects
Overlooking the need for strict preconception and pregnancy control in affected mothers
